events.text: You come down out of your own sky the way rain does, without anyone seeing where it began, and stand on a road in {pw_world} with a hood over your face and dust on your feet. The world does not know you. A carter going the other way nods at you and asks if you are lost. You made the road he is driving on.

choices.text: Say you are only passing through

effects.log: He offers you a ride as far as the next village. The cart is slow. You have never enjoyed anything so much.

choices.text: Ask him what the people pray for

effects.log: "Rain, mostly," he says, "and that the sky would say something for once." You pull the hood lower.

choices.text: Walk on alone

effects.log: The road is longer on foot than it looked from above. Every mile of it is yours, and you feel every one.

events.text: You come down into {pw_world} as a healer with a satchel of herbs and no name anyone has heard. In the first village a child is burning with fever, and the priest has prayed over her for three days. To the god, he says. Nobody above has answered. You put your hand on her forehead and remember that you are the one he was praying to.

choices.text: Heal her the slow way, with herbs

effects.log: It takes all night. In the morning she asks for porridge. The priest thanks the sky, and you let him.

choices.text: Let a little of the god into your hand

effects.log: The fever leaves her at once. The priest stares at you for a long time and says nothing, which is wise of him.

choices.text: Sit with the priest afterwards

effects.log: "Do you think the god hears us?" he asks. You tell him yes. It is the first honest prayer you have ever answered in person.

events.text: You come down into {pw_world} as a teacher, and settle in a village by a river with a slate, a stick of chalk and a borrowed room. On the first morning nine children come to learn their letters. On the second morning one of them asks you who made the world. Everyone laughs. You do not.

choices.text: Tell them a story about it

effects.log: You tell them how the first river was poured. They think you made it up. Some of them will remember it all their lives.

choices.text: Ask them what they think

effects.log: One says a great bird laid it like an egg. One says it was always here. One says nobody made it, and you write that answer on the slate too.

choices.text: Teach them their letters first

effects.log: "Letters first, then the world," you say. They groan. It is the most ordinary morning you have had in an age.

events.text: The road into {pw_world} feels known under your feet, though this life has never walked it. An old woman at a well looks at your hooded face and says, without surprise: "You again. You came last time the sky went quiet too." Some soul of yours has done this before, and the world remembers it better than you do.

choices.text: Ask her what you did last time

effects.log: "You listened," she says. "Nobody else ever did." She fills your water skin and will not take a coin for it.

choices.text: Tell her she is mistaken

effects.log: "Of course," she says, and smiles, and calls you by a name you do not know as you leave.

events.text: Ilo is a shepherd boy of eleven with a sling in his belt and a black eye. He got the eye throwing stones at the false god's priests when they came to take his family's goats for an offering. "Gods are just people with louder voices," he tells you. You ask him if he would like to learn to throw further.

choices.text: Teach him to throw further

effects.log: By the end of the summer he can knock a pine cone off a branch at sixty paces. He has not asked who you are. He will.

choices.text: Teach him to ask why first

effects.log: "Why do they want goats?" you ask him. He thinks about it all the way home. It is a better weapon than the sling.

choices.text: Tell him gods should be quieter, not louder

effects.log: He looks at you strangely. "You talk like you know one," he says.

events.text: Pema is an orphan who sleeps in a temple of yours that everyone else has forgotten. She sweeps it every morning, though nobody comes, and leaves a cup of water on the altar for a god who never drinks it. When you walk in, hooded and dusty, she gives the cup to you instead, because you look thirstier.

choices.text: Drink it

effects.log: It is the best water in the world, and you would know. She asks if you will stay. You say yes, for a while.

choices.text: Ask her why she keeps the temple

effects.log: "Someone should," she says, "in case they come back." You find you cannot say anything for a moment.

choices.text: Sweep the temple with her

effects.log: You sweep it together until the stones shine. It is the first time you have cleaned your own house.

events.text: Tavi is a scribe's apprentice who copies temple records by day and argues with them by night. He has a list of every miracle in the old books with a note beside each one: who saw it, who wrote it down, who was paid. "I do not believe in gods," he tells you, "but I would believe in a good answer." You decide he will get one.

choices.text: Show him a small true thing

effects.log: You make the lamp flame stand still for three breaths. He writes it down, with a question mark. Then he crosses out the question mark.

choices.text: Tell him to keep doubting

effects.log: "Doubt everything I tell you too," you say. He looks delighted. Nobody has ever given him permission before.

choices.text: Help him with his copying

effects.log: Your hand is better than his. He is annoyed about it for a week, and then asks to be taught.

events.text: A boy from the next valley steals one of Ilo's goats, and Ilo catches him at the ford with a stone already in the sling. He looks at you over his shoulder, waiting. He wants to know what you would do. He will do the same thing for the rest of his life.

choices.text: Tell him to let the boy keep it

effects.log: Ilo lowers the sling, furious. Later he finds out the boy's family had nothing to eat, and is quiet for days.

choices.text: Tell him to take it back, and keep his aim

effects.log: Ilo takes it back without a shot. He walks home taller. Something in him learns that strength is the answer.

choices.text: Ask him why the boy stole it

effects.log: Ilo goes to find out. He comes back with the truth, and decides for himself. You are prouder of that than of any aim.

events.text: Ilo is fifteen now, quick and proud, and the other shepherds follow him. One evening he asks you straight out: "When I am grown, should I make them afraid of me, or make them love me?" The fire crackles. He is not joking.

choices.text: Love lasts longer

effects.log: "Fear is quicker," he says. "Love lasts longer," you say again. He sits with that until the fire goes out.

choices.text: Afraid is safer

effects.log: He nods as if he knew. You wonder, walking back, whether you would have said it if you were not so tired.

choices.text: Neither: make them free

effects.log: "Free to leave me?" he asks. "Yes," you say. He does not like it. He thinks about it for years.

events.text: A pilgrim comes to Pema's temple, kneels, and curses the god who made the world for taking her husband. Pema looks at you, white-faced, as if the walls might fall. You are standing right there. The pilgrim does not know you are the one she is cursing.

choices.text: Sit down beside the pilgrim and listen

effects.log: You listen until she has nothing left to say. Pema brings tea. That night Pema says: "So that is what a god is for."

choices.text: Tell Pema the god can bear it

effects.log: "The god can bear it," you say. Pema is not sure she can. She learns to, which is not quite the same.

choices.text: Tell the pilgrim the truth about her husband

effects.log: It was a fever, not a god. She weeps differently after that. Pema learns that the truth can be a kindness too.

events.text: Pema has grown into a quiet young woman who knows every family in the valley by their troubles. She asks you to teach her a miracle, a real one, "so they would believe again". You could. You could give her a small light of your own to carry.

choices.text: Teach her to keep the temple open instead

effects.log: She is disappointed. Then the valley starts coming back, one family at a time, because the door is always open.

choices.text: Give her the small light

effects.log: A little of the god burns in her palm. She is careful with it. People come to see it, and stay to hear her.

choices.text: Tell her who you are

effects.log: She looks at you for a long time, then nods, as if you had told her the weather. "I thought so," she says.

events.text: Tavi has found a temple record that says you, the god of {pw_world}, once drowned a whole kingdom for its pride. It is a lie: you never did. He holds it up. "Did you?" he asks, because he has worked out who you are, and he wants to see what a god does when caught.

choices.text: Say no, and show him the truth gently

effects.log: You show him where the river really ran. He corrects the record in his own hand, and does not gloat.

choices.text: Tell him a god owes nobody an answer

effects.log: He writes that down too. He keeps it for years, the way one keeps a splinter.

choices.text: Tell him: check it yourself

effects.log: He walks a hundred miles to the old riverbed and comes back with mud on his knees and the truth. He is never the same.

events.text: Tavi is a grown scholar now, with students of his own who doubt everything, including him. One of them has written a book saying that Tavi's teacher, the hooded stranger, never existed. Tavi asks you whether he should answer it.

choices.text: Let the book stand

effects.log: "Doubt is how they learned to think," you say. Tavi laughs until he cries. He does not answer the book.

choices.text: Answer it, and win

effects.log: Tavi answers it in four volumes and wins. His school grows. So, a little, does his pride.

choices.text: Answer it with evidence, not with you

effects.log: He answers with records, maps, witnesses. Not a word about gods. It is the best thing he ever writes.

events.text: Two peoples of {pw_world} face each other across a valley of trampled barley, their banners stiff in the wind. You walk out between them with nothing in your hands. Ten thousand spears turn toward one hooded figure. Nobody throws the first one. Then, by the end of the day, nobody wants to.

choices.text: Ask both sides what they are fighting for

effects.log: They tell you. It is the same thing: the valley, their children, the wind. They go home arguing about it, which is better than dying about it.

choices.text: Sit down in the barley and wait

effects.log: You sit until dark. One by one the fires go out on both sides. In the morning there are two armies walking away.

events.text: Two kingdoms of {pw_world} have gathered their armies at a river ford, and their kings are drinking to the battle in their tents. You go to each tent in turn, hooded, a healer with a satchel, and tell each king the same thing about the river: it does not care who wins. You do not know why they listen. You know exactly why.

choices.text: Leave before they can thank you

effects.log: By the time the treaty is signed the healer is gone. Both kingdoms put a hooded figure on their new coins.

choices.text: Stay to see it signed

effects.log: You watch two old men sign a peace with shaking hands. One of them is weeping. The war is over for a generation.

events.text: You walk out between the armies, and this time the first spear is thrown. Then the second. The battle closes over you like water, and a god in a mortal shape is only one body in the mud. You spend the day doing the only thing you can: carrying the wounded out of it, whichever side they are on.

choices.text: Carry them until dark

effects.log: You carry forty out of the field. Both sides will tell of the stranger who would not stop, and neither will know what you were.

choices.text: Stand where you are and let them go round you

effects.log: They go round you, all day, like a river round a stone. You learn something about your world you did not want to know.

events.text: The war does not stop for you. Too much has been burned already, and the people of {pw_world} have stopped believing that anyone, in the sky or on the road, will step in. A soldier pushes you aside without looking. "Go home, old pilgrim," he says. You wonder how long your sky has been empty.

choices.text: Go to the villages behind the lines

effects.log: You spend the season mending roofs and setting bones. It does not stop the war. It stops something.

choices.text: Watch it to the end

effects.log: You watch it all. When you go back up, you will remember every face.

events.text: The false god sits in the great temple of {pw_world} on a throne of your own old offerings, its face a mask of beaten gold. You walk up the steps through its kneeling believers, hooded, and ask it a question nobody has ever asked: "What did you make?" The mask is silent. Then it cracks, top to bottom, and there is nobody behind it.

choices.text: Pick up the pieces of the mask

effects.log: They are only gold. You give them back to the believers, who do not know what to do with them, and then do.

choices.text: Speak to the kneeling crowd

effects.log: "Get up," you say. They do. Some of them look at your hooded face for a long time afterwards.

events.text: Tavi goes up the temple steps beside you with his list of miracles under his arm, and reads it aloud to the false god in front of all its believers: every one of them, who saw it, who wrote it, who was paid. The false god has no answer to a list. By the twentieth miracle the priests are leaving by the side doors.

choices.text: Let Tavi finish the list

effects.log: He reads all two hundred. Nobody is left in the temple but the two of you, and a great many pigeons.

choices.text: Add one true miracle to the end

effects.log: You make every lamp in the temple burn blue at once. Tavi writes it down without a question mark.

events.text: You ask the false god what it made, and it laughs, and its priests drag the hooded stranger down the temple steps while its believers jeer. In a mortal shape you are only a voice, and a voice can be shouted down. The false god holds {pw_world} tonight, and it knows now that someone came for it.

choices.text: Get up and walk away slowly

effects.log: You do not run. A few of the believers notice that, and wonder about it later.

choices.text: Remember every face in the crowd

effects.log: You will remember them. Not in anger. They are yours too, and they have been alone a long time.

events.text: When the priests drag you out of the false god's temple, your disciple does not run. You see them standing on the steps, arguing with a ring of priests, small and stubborn and not afraid, and then the doors close. You wait at the gate until morning. They do not come out.

choices.text: Wait another day

effects.log: You wait three. Nobody comes out. You tell yourself a god knows what happens to everyone. You do not, this time.

choices.text: Go in after them, alone

effects.log: The temple is empty when you get in. Only a sling, or a broom, or a scribe's pen, lies on the floor where they stood.

events.text: You walk a season with the heroes of {pw_world}: the ones its songs are about. They are smaller than the songs, and braver. Around the fire at night they argue about what their god is like. You put another stick on the fire and say nothing, and listen to yourself being described.

choices.text: Tell them the god is probably listening

effects.log: They laugh, and lower their voices anyway. In the morning one of them leaves an extra portion of bread by your pack.

choices.text: Ask them what they would change about the world

effects.log: They have a long list. You remember every item on it. Some of them you will change.

events.text: The heroes of {pw_world} are hunting something that has been taking travellers on the high road. You walk with them, hooded, carrying the lantern. When the thing comes out of the dark, it is only a starving old beast, and the heroes lower their spears without your saying a word. You are very proud of them.

choices.text: Help them feed it

effects.log: The beast follows them for years after. The songs will say they tamed it with a lantern and a kind word. Close enough.

choices.text: Let them decide what to do

effects.log: They argue all night and decide well. You did not make them good. You made a world where they could choose to be.

events.text: {pw_world} has no heroes yet, only people. On a dark road you meet a lantern-bearer named Oren, who walks the night roads between villages so that nobody has to walk them alone. Oren is not afraid of anything, and talks the whole way. You walk beside Oren for a season, and the roads become safer, and then they become a story.

choices.text: Carry the lantern for a night

effects.log: Oren lets you, suspiciously. The light is a little brighter than it should be. Oren does not mention it.

choices.text: Ask Oren why

effects.log: "Somebody should," Oren says. You have heard that answer before, from your own world, and it never stops being true.

events.text: In every village you pass the temples are half empty. "The sky has gone quiet," a farmer tells you, not angry, only tired. "We pray, and nothing comes back. Not even weather." You are standing right in front of him. Above you, your heaven is an empty room.

choices.text: Pray with him

effects.log: You pray to yourself beside him. It is the strangest thing you have ever done, and it helps, a little, both of you.

choices.text: Tell him it will not be quiet for ever

effects.log: He shrugs. "Nothing is," he says, and goes back to his plough.

events.text: With its sky gone quiet, the false god of {pw_world} grows bold. Its priests stand on every crossroads now, saying the old god is dead and they have the bones to prove it. A crowd gathers. Nobody argues. You stand at the back of the crowd, very much alive, and listen to your own funeral.

choices.text: Ask the priest to show the bones

effects.log: He cannot, of course. Two people in the crowd notice, and start asking the same question in other villages.

choices.text: Walk away before you say something

effects.log: You walk a long way before you trust your voice. The false god will have to wait for its answer.

events.text: The lesser gods of your heaven keep the temples while you are gone. A shrine of {pw_lgod} stands open at a crossroads with fresh flowers on it, and an old woman tells you the god of {pw_ldomain} has been very kind lately, kinder than the great god ever was. You find you do not mind at all.

choices.text: Leave a flower at the shrine yourself

effects.log: Somewhere above you, a god you raised notices, and does not know who left it.

choices.text: Ask her what the great god was like

effects.log: "Distant," she says. "Like weather." You resolve to be a little less like weather.

events.text: A storm comes to {pw_world} that nobody sent. Without you in the sky it goes where it likes, and it likes a fishing village on the east shore. You are there, in a mortal shape, with a mortal's two hands. You do what mortals do in a storm. You hold on to the people next to you.

choices.text: Hold on until it passes

effects.log: It passes. Everyone in your row of the boathouse lives. You never felt so small, or so needed.

choices.text: Help them rebuild after

effects.log: You stay a month, hauling timber. The village builds a little shrine to the stranger who stayed. It is the wrong shape. It is perfect.

events.text: You climb the last hill of the road and step back up into your heaven, and {pw_world} is full of light again. Below, people come out of their houses and look up without knowing why. You stopped a war, unmasked a lie, walked with its heroes. Your sky has never felt less empty.

choices.text: Look down at the roads you walked

effects.log: You can see every one of them from here. They looked shorter from above. You will never think so again.

choices.text: Rest a moment before you speak to the world

effects.log: For a moment you are only tired, in a good way, like a farmer after a harvest.

events.text: You go back up into your heaven. Below, your disciple stands on a hill and watches the sky fill with light, and understands at last who taught them, and does not wave, and does not need to. They have a long life ahead of them, and work to do. You will be watching.

choices.text: Send them a sign

effects.log: A single bird lands on their shoulder and stays a moment. Your disciple laughs out loud on the empty hill.

choices.text: Leave them to their work

effects.log: You owe them that: to be trusted. They will become what they become. That is what you taught them.

events.text: You go back up into your heaven alone. Somewhere below, behind the closed doors of a temple, your disciple did not come out. A god who can see everything can see that too. It is the first grief your world has given you, and you carry it up with you.

choices.text: Keep a light burning for them

effects.log: In the sky of {pw_world} there is a new star nobody can explain. You know its name.

choices.text: Promise the world it will not happen again

effects.log: It is a promise only a god could make, and only a god could break. You mean it.

events.text: The mortal shape wears thin, and you step back up into your heaven. Below, the people of {pw_world} look up at a sky that is full again and are not sure anything changed. Perhaps nothing did. You walked its roads, and you know it better than you ever did from here.

choices.text: Remember the faces

effects.log: You remember all of them: the carter, the children, the old woman at the well. A god with a memory is a different god.

choices.text: Go back to your work

effects.log: You turn to the year that waits, a little wiser and a little sorer, the way anyone comes home.

events.text: Ilo comes up the stair of your heaven with a sling still in his belt, grey now, and stands in front of the seat you have made for him, and grins. "So it was you," he says. "All those years." Then he sits down, and the shepherds of {pw_world} feel the wind change in their favour.

choices.text: Ask him what kind of god he will be

effects.log: "A loud one," he says, and then, more quietly, "a fair one." You believe the second more.

choices.text: Give him the sling back, blessed

effects.log: He spins it once and a star moves. He will have to be careful. He knows it.

events.text: Pema comes up the stair of your heaven carrying a cup of water, the way she did the first day, and puts it on the arm of her new seat. "In case you are thirsty," she says. Below, every forgotten temple in {pw_world} has its door open by morning, and nobody knows who opened them.

choices.text: Drink it

effects.log: It is still the best water in the world. She smiles. The heaven feels like a house for the first time.

choices.text: Tell her to drink it herself

effects.log: "Gods are thirsty too," you say. She laughs, and drinks, and is a god.

events.text: Tavi comes up the stair of your heaven with a notebook, and before he sits down he asks you three questions about how heaven works. You answer two. He writes "unknown" beside the third, satisfied, and takes his seat. The scholars of {pw_world} start finding their arguments a little easier to settle.

choices.text: Answer the third question too

effects.log: He crosses out "unknown" and looks disappointed. He liked it better with a mystery in it.

choices.text: Tell him to keep the notebook open

effects.log: "Always," he says. You suspect he will be the most useful god you ever raised.

events.text: In a dream you are walking a road in {pw_world} with a hood over your face, and a carter going the other way asks if you are lost. You wake with dust on your feet that was not there when you lay down. Some life of yours walked among them. It is still walking, somewhere in you.

choices.text: Go and look at your world tonight

effects.log: It is still there, turning, and somewhere on it a carter is telling the story of a stranger who was not lost.

choices.text: Shake the dust out of your shoes

effects.log: You keep a little of it in a twist of paper. You could not say why.

events.text: One of the gods of your heaven bows when this life of yours turns to {pw_world}, a little deeper than the others, the way a student bows to a teacher. You do not remember teaching anyone. Your soul does. It bows back.

choices.text: Ask the god how you met

effects.log: The god tells you about a hooded stranger, a village, a long summer. You listen as if to a story about someone else. It is not.

choices.text: Bow back, and say nothing

effects.log: Some things do not need to be remembered to be true.

events.text: The old people of {pw_world} tell a story on long nights: once, when the sky went quiet, a hooded stranger walked the roads and nobody knew who it was. An old woman of the village says the stranger once shared her grandmother's bread. Everyone's grandmother says that. You find yourself believing every one of them.

choices.text: Ask what the stranger looked like

effects.log: "Nobody saw the face," the old woman says. "That was the point." You think about that for a long time.

choices.text: Pull your hood up, for fun

effects.log: The little ones scream with delight. An old man by the fire does not laugh, and looks at you for a long time.

events.text: There is a shrine in the hills to a god who was once a mortal of {pw_world}: a disciple of the hooded stranger, they say, taught face to face and raised into the sky. Pilgrims leave small things there, a stone, a cup of water, a page of notes. You leave something too, without knowing why your hands are shaking.

choices.text: Kneel

effects.log: The wind stops for a moment, the way it does when someone is listening.

choices.text: Read the old carving on the shrine

effects.log: It says: "Taught in person. Do the same." You decide that you will.

events.text: In the valley of trampled barley, where two peoples of {pw_world} nearly went to war long ago, there is a stone with no name on it, only the shape of a hooded figure sitting down. Children dare each other to sit in its lap. The story says nobody fought that day because a stranger sat in the barley and would not get up.

choices.text: Sit in its lap

effects.log: It is warm, though the day is cold. You sit there until the other children get bored and go home.

choices.text: Ask whose side the stranger was on

effects.log: "Nobody's," says the oldest child, scornfully. "That was the point." Everyone says that about the stranger.
